Crime against tourists ि
*t l61.    SHRIMATI PREMA CARlAPPA:tt SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ: 
Will the Minister of TOURISM be pleased to state: 
(a)  whether Government has taken note of increasing cases of crime against tourists at tourist centres; 
(b)  whether Government has under its consideration a mechanism to prevent crimes against tourists; and 
(c)  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the table of 
the Sabha. 
Statement  
(a) to (c) 'Public Order' and 'Police' are State subjects as per the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India. 
As such, the prevention of crime, including crimes against tourists, is the primary responsibility of State 
Governments/Union Territories. Following recent reports in the media regarding harassment and misbehaviour with 
tourists in India, the Ministry of Tourism discussed the issue of safety and security of tourists, amongst other 
issues, with Secretaries of Tourism of States/Union Territories. The Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of 
Defence. During this meeting the feasibility of deploying the ex-servicemen as Tourist Wardens in States and 
Union Territories was also discussed. It was emphasised that ensuring the safety and security of tourists is of 
paramount importance and State Governments/Union Territories must ensure the same. 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Sir, late Jawaharlal Nehru said that tourists are our 'honoured guests'. 
We say, "srfafs* ^cft *rai" But it is alarming to read reports in the newspapers about the increasing number of 
attacks on foreign tourists in the tourist-important places, especially, Rajasthan and Goa, which attract maximum 
tourists. Sir, both Rajasthan and Goa are increasingly becoming unsafe for the tourists and it will tarnish the image 
of India in the eyes of Europe, America and the rest of the world. Therefore, 1 would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether there is any mechanism to put an end to such attacks on tourists. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, I would have to begin necessarily with the reply, even though I run the risk of 
sounding casual about it which I am not, that law and order comes under every State Government under the 
Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. But having said that we are absolutely aware of the fact that India has its great 
tradition of "srfcTf*? t<*t W, and it is enhancing the prestige and the importance of this legacy which we 
have.

Today, we can proudly say that from 2004, from 3.42 million tourists, we were able to have 5 million 
inbound tourists by the 31st of December, 2007. Before I answer the hon. Member's question, I would 
also like to say that the Finance Minister is sitti ng here — we have, in the year 2007, been able to 
contribute 12 billion US dollars to the national ex chequer. We are holding and continuing to work 
for the goal that tourism provides the largest amou nt of direct and indirect employment. While the 
worldwise statistics is 8.3 per cent towards employment from tourism, in India, we proudly claim 
that direct and indirect employment flowing out of tourism is 8.9 per cent. 
Having said that, Sir, we are conscious of the fact that when tourists come from different parts of 
the world to a country, in an open society, they can go anywhere and visit any place they would like to 
visit. We have been constantly writing to the State Governments, constantly emphasising over the years 
with the State Governments to set up a 'Special Tou rism Police'. I am happy to say that ten State 
Governments did adhere to this suggestion of ours from the Centre and have set up a 'Tourism Police'. 
Some have constituted a separate Tourism Police and  some have drawn out of the normal police 
force and other security services and constituted a  'Tourist Police Force'. It is true, especially sin ce 
the last days of December 2007, till date, several incidents have come to light through the media and 
otherwise, where women tourists, particularly, have been harassed and exploited; and there have been 
rapes and there have also been security lapses. I would like to say that we had a meeting on the 24th 
of January. It was called for the purpose of infras tructure development, but we put the safety of 
inbound tourists and domestic tourists as the Item No. 1 on the agenda. The Home Ministry and the 
Defence Ministry were represented there. After discussing the issue with the representatives of all the 
States that were present, we have suggested the for mation of a Tourism Task Force comprising of 
retired Army personnel. We know that our jawans and others retire somewhere at the age of 28 or 32 
years; they have a certain credibility in the minds  of the people: they have a sense of discipline. So, 
we have drawn out a structure and the blueprint of that structure has been cleared by the Ministries of 
Home and Defence to the extent that they have no ob jection to the setting up of this force. We have 
sent it to the State Governments with the proposal to put in place at the earliest possible 
opportunity. Alongside this, I am sure the hon. Mem bers are aware that the Ministry at the Centre 
at regular intervals projects 'sensitisation short films' on television whereby we sensitise people like 
tourist guides, taxi drivers and others who come in contact with the tourists in how to behave, how to 
deal with the tourists in a dignified way in a mann er that it behoves our concept of 'atithi devo 
bhavah'. These are the four or five steps which we have take n from the Centre in addition to the 
advisories which are issued on a regular basis by private operators. 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Sir, the "incredible India' campaign has been successful. If the 
Government does not make tourism safe, then the cam paign will lose its credibility. The hon. 
Minister has already said that the Government will set up a special task force for tourists. I would like 
to know from the hon. Minister whether the crime rate in respect of tourists has increased or 
decreased over the past three years. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, I would like to inform the hon. Member that we do not have any 
tabulated figures. But I did access some figures wh ich have been printed and widely circulated by 
the Home Ministry. There was a recent World Economi c Forum Report which mentioned certain 
figures and which we have contradicted except the f igures pertaining to accidents on roads which

DR. PC. ALEXANDER: Sir, I am afraid the reply given  by the hon. Minister may not result in 
the right solution for the problem that we have raised. May I invite the attention of the hon., Minister 
to the fact that a task force constituted by ex-ser vicemen will not be the same as the police force. I f 
this problem has to be tackled effectively, there h as to be a dedicated police force. Will the hon. 
Minister try to get from the Finance Ministry a matching contribution even to the extent of 75 per cen t 
of the additional cost which the State Government m ay have to incur in creating Special Task Police 
Force as distinguished from the group of ex-service  Personnel that you have mentioned? Sir, the 
problem is not just a law and order problem. It has become customary for us to listen to this elementary 
lesson in politics and constitutional law that subject of Law and order is a State subject. But tourism is 
of utmost importance to the nation as a whole becau se the reputation of the nation is involved and, 
therefore, I urge the hon. Minister to take steps f or creating a dedicated task force of the police an d 
give an assurance to us that she will move in that direction instead of depending upon ex-
servicemen. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, I quite agree with the hon. Member that we cannot depend on 
any one particular category of people to be recruit ed. This is normally the prerogative of the State 
Governments and I am not shifting either the blame or responsibility. I do fully realise that the campaign 
for increased tourism has been driven by the Centre  with the full collaboration of the State 
Governments and the private sector and I am taking that share of the responsibility on us at the 
Centre. But this task force has been suggested in a ddition to the tourism police, which, I earlier 
mentioned, has already been set up by ten States. S ome States replied that they don't have this 
problem and they don't need tourism police and some States are looking into the proposal now. This 
task force is suggested as an additional force whic h will man those monuments which are most 
visited and for some special purposes where people may require help like beaches, railway stations, 
bus stops, etc., where domestic and in-bound tourists do frequent. But I will take the hon. Member's 
suggestion and I am sure the Finance Minister, who happens to be present, can help us

SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Sir, as Prema Cariappaji said and she is feeling that Goa 
has become unsafe. This is the impression largely by media by blowing only one case throughout for 
the last four or five days. We do sympathise with t he girl who was murdered on the beach of Goa. 
But, Sir, it is the responsibility of others also, members of the family also, to see whether young girls as 
small as fifteen years of age should be allowed to move freely in the midnight on the beaches of Goa. In 
this context, Sir, I would like to know whether the Ministry of Tourism is going to issue any advisory 
to tourists or would like to advise the State Government to issue any advisory to tourists. 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, the hon. Member certainly has a point if he is particularly referring to 
the most recent incident which has been highlighted continuously over the last few days by the media. 
We are talking about the minor girl who, unfortunately, lost her life. People are talking of the fact that

this time, not go into that aspect and look at how we can strengthen our system where people even

SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Sir, I was going to ask anot her question, but now, considering

(a)  whether it is a fact that some illegal construction s have come up through nexus between

officials? ,

well as from local administration is sought by lodging a complaint and by registering an FIR, followed 
by an order to the District Collector/Magistrate fr om Director General, Archaeological Survey of 
India to remove such illegal/unauthorized construct ion under Rule 38 of the AMASR Rules, 1959. If 
the above procedure fails to yield any fruitful results and the State Government also fails in removin g 
the unauthorized/illegal constructions, legal action is taken by filing cases in the Law courts. 
SHRIMATI HEM A MALINI: Sir, I would like to know fr om the hon. Minister whether the 
Government have a competent team of research schola rs who can guide the proper and aesthetic 
restoration of our monuments. We have seen in some parts of our historical sites that restoration has 
been done in a very ugly manner in spite of the ASI  being there. The case in point is that of the 
world famous Ajanta Caves. Recently, construction o f a cement portico in front of the Cave was 
somehow permitted. But, fortunately, it was stopped due to protest from conservationists. Do all the 
historical monuments, small or big, come under the ASI jurisdiction? Many smaller monuments are in 
an extremely dilapidated condition around the country. What is the yardstick the ASI adopts to select 
and preserve the monuments? What are the powers given to the ASI to prevent vandalism? Does the 
ASI collaborate with UNESCO's World Heritage Foundation? 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, this question is so different. I am so sorry, while I could answer the 
hon. Member, but her question specifically deals wi th illegal constructions near Humayun Tomb. 
And, if I have to answer on Maharashtra's Ajanta-Ellora Caves or on the UNESCO or another issue, 
either you would have to frame your question differently. But, I can try and answer the hon. Member 
to the extent I have knowledge of the whole subject. 
She talked of our restoration work in Ajanta-Ellora  Caves. That has been done according to 
specifications certified by experts who come in from UNESCO and monitor all restoration work on World 
Heritage Sites. And, there have been photographs taken without flashlights which are not allowed inside 
the two Caves. I would recommend to the hon. Member, whenever she has time to visit some of these 
exhibitions and a collection which we have access to, she could see for herself the restoration work in 
these two caves which is quite praiseworty. 
As far as monuments are concerned, the ASI has 3,776 monuments of national importance under their 
care. Annually a plan is made for restoration work and allocation of funds for the work to be done at 
these monuments. There are about 3,500 monuments wh ich are under the care of the State 
Governments. Altogether we look at about 7,000 monu ments divided between the ASI and the 
State Governments. Work is done according to the su rveys and the monitoring takes place at regular 
intervals. We have students preparing in our instit utes to undertake work of archaeological 
restoration and conservation. I am very happy to in form the House that we did with great worldwide 
acclaim the restoration work of the entire Angkor-Vat Temple in Cambodia. So much so that thereafter 
we have been accessed by the Governments of Indonesia, Cambodia and Singapore to do restoration 
work in their countries as well. If there are any other questions outside the Humayun Tomb, then.... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please be specific to the main question. 
SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Sir, does the Government have an agenda to create awareness and instil 
pride in the people, especially those living in close proximity in these irreplaceable structures? 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Sir, it is very unfortunate t hat over the years, due to 
developmental processes, our monuments in many places have been encroached upon.

The ASI with its limited staff and our Superintendi ng Archaeologists in different States, as soon as 
they get to know that there is an encroachment or a  building is higher and blocks and view of the 
monument, because we follow the law and rules of 19 58 and then the rules of 1959, we do send a 
notice to those who are violating building laws. Wh en they don't listen, we file a complaint with the 
District Collector and ask him to use the police or security forces to get that vacated. And, failing all 
this, we also file cases. I have a list, which I can provide to the hon. Member later, of all the cases we 
have filed over the years; the cases where we have achieved some measure of success and the cases 
where we are still trying to get these places vacated. 
But I would like to mention here that some of our r ules are found today to be a little bit irational. 
We are looking at the 1959 Act which lays down the rules and the 1992 Act, and trying to look at the 
modern demands of development and also preservation and conservation of archaeological heritage. 
We are trying to rationalize these laws. I have put in place a Committee of five eminent experts who 
look into this field besides the ASI.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Honourable Members, I have an announc ement to make. We have 
with us seated in the Special Box, Members of a Par liamentary Delegation from Slovakia, 
currently on a visit to our country under the disti nguished leadership of His Excellency Mr. 
Pavol Paska, Speaker of the National Council of the Slovak Republic.  
On behalf of the Members of the House and on my own  behalf, I take pleasure in 
extending a hearty welcome to the leader and other Members of the delegation and wish our 
distinguished guests an enjoyable and fruitful stay  in our country. We hope that during their 
stay here, they would be able to see and learn more  about our Parliamentary system, our

bonds that exist between India and Slovakia. Through them, we convey our greetings and best 
wishes to the Parliament and the friendly people of Slovakia.

Full utilisation of runways at airport 
♦163.      PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: SHRI 
VIJAY J. DARDA:tt 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
 whether the Directorate General of Civil Aviation plans to maximize utilisation of runways at 
major airports around the country; 
 if so, whether proper infrastructure is available at major airports to make utilization of runways; 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 to what extent the major airports would be modernized to have full utilization of runways? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): 
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (d) In order to make maximum use of runways,  all the major airports are equipped with 
Navigational Aids i.e. Instrument Landing System (ILS), Distance Measuring Equipment (DME), Very 
High Frequency Omni Range (VOR), runway lightings, Approach Lighting System, RADAR, VHF 
frequencies. Advanced Surface Movement Guidance and  Control System (ASMGCS) has been 
installed at Delhi airport and is being planned for  Mumbai, Chennaiand Kolkata airport. Besides, 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) has initiated maj or development works for 
modernisation/upgradation of airports. These includ e construction of parallel taxi track and link 
taxiways to maximise the utilisation of runways as well as increasing the length of runway wherever 
required.

12   Oral Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
MR. CHAIRMAN: What is the supplementary question? O ne question, please. You get two 
questions, Dardaji. Please ask them one by one. 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Okay, Sir. Why departures of many flights are delayed even after boarding 
by passengers on an announcement made by the ground -handling staff giving the "Ready for 
Departure" signal? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, there are many parts of the question, but, I think, broadly speaking, 
what the hon. Member is referring to is the congest ion which is prevailing at major airports in our 
country. And of course, there is no denying the fact that especially in Mumbai and Delhi, the two major 
airports which handle the maxium number of traffic, we are witnessing delays on account of both arrivals 
and departures. Sir, just to give a little idea of the kind of activity which has been taken place in the 
aviation, in 2004, Delhi used to handle, approximately, 300 plus flights a day, which has now gone up 
to almost 675 flights a day. And in Mumbai, the sit uation is no different. It was, approximately, 350 
flights a day in 2004. Now, it is more than 725 or 750 flights a day. It just goes to show that the 
number of movements in the air has gone up and the corresponding infrastructure is yet to be 
developed to the levels which an handle this volume  of traffic. That notwithstanding, we are all 
aware that the modernisation and upgradation proces s of all airports across the country is going on. 
Major airports, of course, are getting more, I woul d say, investments. The other small airports, in 
anticipation of future growth, are also being upgraded. But, at the same time, 1 would like to inform all 
the Members that while we are handling this growth, we are also very conscious of the fact that high 
growth and high traffic results in more pressure on the system. Safety, being of paramount concern, 
has also to be given due emphasis. All those parameters are being well addressed. 
As regards the ATCs, 1 would like to inform that from 1999, for whatever reason, till 2004 we had a 
recruitment ban and, on the other, the requirement of ATCs went up. Since 2004 we have been 
constantly recruiting. Recruitment does not mean th at it is the end of it. They have to be duly 
trained with the intention to handle the high volum e of traffic safety. That is now being done. Apart 
from that, we have also gone beyond the handling of this additional traffic. Earlier, only one runway 
used to be used in Mumbai and Delhi. We don't have parallel runways as yet. But we are now using 
cross runway in Mumbai and the second runway in Del hi for a substantial period of time and as a 
result the capacity of the runways has increased. W hen I say that the number of movements almost 
doubled within a span of three years, it also natur ally means that we have to take recourse to using 
the secondary runways to be able to handle this vol ume of traffic. Yes, there is traffic congestion. 
Maybe, it is phenomenon new to us in India. All ove r the world, I am sure, where most of us 
travelled, we do find congestion in major airports,  though they have two, three or four runways. 
Ultimately, the pressure will be according to the v olume of traffic and, especially at peak hours, in 
major airports all over the world congestion on the  ground or in the air is quite a common feature. 
That doesn't mean that we should continue with the way it is. We have to, of course, upgrade our 
infrastructure. The Government is moving in that direction. 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Sir, in my first question, I have asked about the fuel consumption which he 
has not replied to. ...(Interruptions)... Bagrodiaji has some objection. ...(Interruptions)... My next 
question is relating to security. ...(Interruptions)...  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please put your question. 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Are there checking at the coun ters, at the x-ray machines, emigration 
counters, customs counters, security counters, etc.? Are they in position as per 

Oral Answers  [11 MARCH, 2008]  to Questions    13 
internationally acceptable standards? You must have notices security lapses on the runways, as well as, 
in the main buildings. Today anybody can buy a tick et for Rs. 30 and go with a passenger. As you 
know, they are not searched. Anybody can come, keep a bag, blow it and go. I have seen lack of 
security. 
The second thing is this. Yesterday, you must have seen a report in the Press that one deer was 
found on the runway at Nagpur airport. There was a nilgai on the runway at Kanpur airport; there 
were some dogs on the runway at Mumbai airport. What kind of security are you having? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, as regards the earlier part  of the question, fuel burnt, no accurate 
statistics are available as to how much is the fuel burnt on account of holding the flights in the air or 
on the ground. But, at the same time, we must accep t that delays or holding flights in the air cause 
loss in terms of fuel burnt to airlines. It is a Na tional loss. Nobody is denying that. But to give th e 
accurate figures would not be probably, possible. 
As regards the measures of security at airports, I think, we are all very sensitive to the issues of 
security, especially in the context of our own country, where we do face terrorism on an ongoing basis 
and across all States virtually. So, security of airports is a very important aspect. The Bureau of Civil 
Aviation Security has been given this responsibility. They act in accordance with the inputs which they 
get from the agencies from time to time. I am not saying that we have any fool-proof arrangement; I 
don't think that is anyway possible. At the same ti me, to the best of whatever is possible, I think the 
Indian airports are relatively manned in that fashion. I am sure if there is any issue which needs to be 
looked into, it will be addressed. And the concern, which the hon. Member has raised, will, of course, 
be given due attention. At the same time, you must also appreciate that the volume of traffic has 
increased; we had almost 95 million passengers this year. It is a very large number, and I am sure, it also 
puts that much pressure on the system. But we will address it. In terms of some stray incidents of deer 
going into the periphery, I think, the perimeter se curity, in our context, is becoming very important. 
And, it is not only the question of deer or nilgai; I am sure no animal or human being should be able to 
enter the airport periphery. That is why, in our future programme, perimeter security is a very important 
aspect. And, as I said earlier, in terms of security and other concerns, including terrorism and all other 
issues, we will be addressing the perimeter securit y. I would say, in a very, very hi-tech manner. 
Already specifications are being put in place so th at perimeter security becomes absolutely fool-
proof. 
SHRI SU. THIRUNAVUKKARASAR: Sir, at the Tiruchirapalli airport, there is only one Airway 
which is functioning. The private airline, Air Deccan, had applied for permission to operate flights from

SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: I am not aware of this particular incident. But I do not see any reason that 
if an airline wishes to operate in any city, lack o f security personnel could be the factor. Trichy is  
already an operational airport, and it has quite a few flights. It is not in isolation.

SHRI R. SHUNMUGASUNDARAM: Sir, according to me, utilisation and modernisation of runway 
along will not help in handling the increasing numb er of flights and passenger movement in the

then, you can decongest the traffic at the Chennai airport. 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, what I could gather from the hon. Member's statement is that we should 
encourage more infrastructure in level-II cities also. 
SHRI R. SHUNMUGASUNDARAM: That would decongest the airport. 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: That would decongest. Well, of course, I think the growth of aviation is 
not only happening in Mumbai and Delhi. I could not give you accurate statistics but, broadly speaking, 
the share of Mumbai and Delhi, only these two airports, vis-a-vis the total aviation traffic in the country 
in 2004 was almost as high as 65 per cent of the to tal. Now, that share has come down well under 50 
per cent; it would be close to 40 per cent. It just  shows that the traffic pattern in our country has 
changed. It is not only concentrated in Mumbai and Delhi but other cities also. In fact, in 2004, there 
were 50 operational airports in the country which received commercial flights. That number has gone 
up to almost 82. So, it is a conscious effort of the Government. Besides this, we have also encouraged 
regional airlines as a concept because we never had a regional airlines permit. We only used to have 
national operators permit; now, we have a regional operators *permit. That also gets incentives; landing and 
parking fees are waived for 80-seater and below air craft. The hon. Finance Minister has already 
declared goods status to fuel for aircraft below 80  seats and that, in a way, will promote regional 
connectivity exactly on the lines that you are sayi ng. Again, iti is a demand-supply situation. As 
airports are available, airlines are available, nat urally they would try to find markets where they 
would get passengers.

Committee on merger of Public Sector Banks  
t*164. MISS ANUSUIYA UIKEY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 whether any Committee had been constituted by Government to suggest the merging of Public 
Sector Banks; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether the report has been submitted to Government by the Committee; 
 if so, when was it submitted; 
 the names of Banks proposed to be merged on the bas is of this report and the reasons of this 
merging; and 
 by when the procedure for merging would be completed and what would be its benefits? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (f) A statement is laid on the 
table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (d) Government had, in August 1991, constitu ted a high level Committee on the financial 
system to examine all aspects relating to the struc ture, organization, functions and procedures of 
financial system under the Chairmanship of Shri M. Narasimham. The Committee had submitted its 
report in November 1991 to the Government. In Decem ber 1997, Government had further 
constituted a high level Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri M. Narasimham on banking sector 
reforms to review the record of implementation of f inancial system reforms recommended by the 
Narasimham Committee in its earlier report and to chart the reforms necessary in the years ahead so 
that India's banking sector can become stronger and  better equipped to compete effectively in a fast 
changing international economic environment. The Second Committee had also submitted its report 
on banking sector reforms to the Government in April 1998. The Committee on banking sector reforms 
(Narasimham Committee) had, inter-alia, recommended consolidation in the banking sector as part of 
wider financial sector reforms. 
(e) and (f) Government is of the view that any proposal for consolidation, by way of merger etc., of 
one public sector bank with another public sector bank, should emanate from the concerned bank with 
Government playing a supportive role. The respective boards of directors of State Bank of lndia and State 
Bank of Saurashtra have approved merger of both banks to allow economies of scale in terms of network, 
man-power and other resources, besides entailing better management of risks. The proposal is under 
examination in Government.

Civil Aviation Agreement between India and Pakistan 
t*165.    MS. SUSHILA TIRIYA: SHRI 
MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
 the matters on which discussions were held recently between Civil Aviation officials of India 
and Pakistan; 
 whether a decision was taken to increase the number of flights from 12 to 28 in a week and to link 
Chennai and Islamabad by air route to boost mutual relationship among the citizens of India and 
Pakistan in this mutual talk; 
 the names of airlines which have applied for providing flights to Pakistan; and 
 the names of airlines permitted to ply between Indi a and Pakistan and the criteria adopted 
for the same? 
t Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.  

Written Answers to  [11 MARCH, 2008]  Starred Questions    19 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): 
(a) to (d) Bilateral air services consultations between India and Pakistan were held on 14-15 February, 
2008 at Rawalpindi in Pakistan. As per the MOU signed between the two sides during the talks, the 
capacity entitlements for the designated airlines of each side have been increased from 12 flights per 
week to 28 flights per week. Also, Islamabad and Chennai have been granted as additional points of 
call for the designated airlines of India and Pakistan respectively. 
As per the agreement reached during the above talks , each side could now designate up to three 
airlines. At present, Indian Airlines is the only d esignated Indian carrier and Pakistan International 
Airlines, Shaheen Air International and Air Blue are the designated airlines of Pakistan. 
Derivatives Trading by Indian Banks 
* 166. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRA SEKHAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 the quantum of derivatives trading and exposure on Indian stock market by Indian banks with 
their own capital during the last three years ending 31st December, 2007, year-wise and bank-wise, 
and 
 what systematic safeguards are in place to prevent the recurrence of any large scale losses 
arising from derivatives trading like the one recently reported in France by Societe Generale? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) As per the extant guidelines 
of Reserve Bank of India (RBI), equity derivatives are not in the list of permissible derivative instruments 
that may be transacted by the banks. Bank-wise stat ements indicating total outstanding notional 
principal amount of derivatives and outstanding direct investment by Indian banks in capital market for 
the last three years as at end December 2005,2006 a nd 2007 are given in the statement-I and 
statement II respectively. 
(b) To provide a framework for undertaking derivati ves transactions from a regulatory 
perspective, RBI has issued comprehensive guidelines on derivatives on 20th April, 2007 enunciating 
the broad principles and major requirements for und ertaking derivative transactions, such as the 
participants, purpose, eligibility criteria to unde rtake such transactions, permissible derivative 
instruments/products, etc. The guidelines also set out • basic principles of a prudent system to control 
the risks arising out of derivative transactions as also on corporate governance aspects. As per these  
guidelines, the banks have to put in place a Board approved policy framework for derivative 
transactions, to ensure, inter-alia, that the policy is consistent with the strategic ob jectives, capital 
strength and management capabilities of the institu tion, to hedge or transfer risks effectively, 
efficiently and expeditiously. RBI has been vested with extensive powers of supervision, regulation 
and control over the commercial banks through the B anking Regulation Act, 1949 and Reserve Bank 
of India Act, 1934. The main instruments of supervi sion and monitoring over the banks are through 
'On-site inspection' and 'Off-site monitoring and s urveillance'. During On-site inspections, RBI 
assesses the adherence by the bank to the regulator y guidelines on risk management systems as well 
as their ability to identify, measures, monitor and manage all types of risks, besides the adequacy and 
effectiveness of the internal control and systems in the bank.

Reduction of bulk  LPG supply by RIL to IOC  
* 167.      SHRI MOHAMMED AMIN: 
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
 whether recent LPG shortage in the country was also due to reduction in bulk LPG supplies by 
Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL) in the month of Janu ary, 2008 to Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) and 
other public sector oil marketing companies; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether there are any penal provisions in case of such abrupt reduction of supply by RIL 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA): (a) and (b) At 
present, there is no overall shortage of LPG in the  country. Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) have reported that they have supplied 8,450 TMT (thousand metric tonnes) of domestic LPG 
in the country during the period April' 07-January '08 as against 8,030 TMT during the 
corresponding period of last year, showing a growth of 5.2%. 
During the month of January '08 the actual LPG production at RIL, Jamnagar refinery was 236.97 
TMT against the planned production of 240 TMT. This shortfall in production of about 3 TMT was 
marginal as the supplies from PSU refineries/fracto nators during January '08 was 522 TMT. The 
backlog in LPG supplies in some States of the country during the month of January '08 was due to a 
combination of factors viz: Production of reduced/ off-spec LPG at some of the sources, delay in 
movement of bulk LPG by rail, delay in berthing of vessels at Haldia Port, increase in demand in 
some of the States due to the severe cold resulting in panic refill booking by customers, strikes and go 
slow agitations by contract labour in IOC plants in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal. 
(c) to (e) At present, supply of LPG in RIL is being made under a "Product Off Take Agreement" 
signed between IOC and RIL which is valid up to 31.03.09. As per the agreement, IOC is to advise its 
deficit LPG for the financial year to RIL and subject to availability of LPG with them, RIL shall have the 
first right of supply to IOCL. Under the agreementR IL will indicate the price for supply of LPG. 
However, if IOC demonstrates to RIL that IOC can pu rchase LPG from other sources at lower rates 
than those offered by RIL, IOC will have the option to require RIL to match such price and in case of 
refusal, IOC will have the option to buy LPG from other sources.

* 168. MS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of CORP ORATE AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) how many companies have made preferential allot ments either to promoters or other private 
groups during the last three years; 

Written Answers to  [11 MARCH, 2008]  Starred Questions   27 
(b) how many companies have sought shareholders' ap proval for such preferential 
allotments through postal ballot mechanism and through general body meeting; 
(c) whether Government is contemplating to stop thi s method of preferential allotment to 
promoters through postal allotment as it hurts the small investors whose value of share 
gets diluted; 
.(d) whether Government has any plans to do so; and 
(e) if so, by when; and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CORPORATE AFFAIRS (SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA): (a)and (b) The 
information is being collected and will be laid on the Table of the House. 
(c) As per provisions of section 81 (1 A) of the Co mpanies Act, 1956, further shares can be 
offered by a company to any person(s) (whether exis ting members or not), in any manner, if 
the company passes a special resolution to this eff ect, or, if the company passes an ordinary 
resolution and obtains Government approval thereto.  Allotment of shares made in such 
manner to a select group of persons and not to publ ic at large is also termed as preferential 
allotment. 
In terms of provisions of section 192A of the Companies Act, 1956, a listed company may voluntarily 
pass resolutions under section 81 (1 A) of the Companies Act, 1956 for preferential allotment by way of 
postal ballot. 
Further, SEBI (Disclosure & Investor Protection) Gu idelines, 2000 regulate various aspects of 
preferential allotment by listed companies such as pricing of the issue, currency of financial 
instruments, non-transferability of financial instr uments, the validity period of shareholders' 
resolution etc. 
Since the price at which shares are offered in a preferential allotment by a listed company, is fixed as 
per SEBI Guidelines, there is a regulatory safeguar d against the value of shares held by small 
investors being selectively devalued. 
(d) and (e) The mechanism of postal ballot enables wider shareholder participation in the 
company resolutions. Such participation would make the decision taken by such resolution 
more democratic. In view of this, there is no propo sal to do away with this method of 
ascertaining the consent of shareholders. In case o f any oppression and mismanagement 
by the company, the aggrieved minority shareholders  may approach the Company Law 
Board for relief under section 397/398, read with section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b)The investments of the co-
operative banks are regulated by the RBI's circular s issued from time to time. As per the extant 
circular of RBI, keeping in view the various regula tory/statutory and the bank's own internal 
requirements, co-operative banks are required to la y down, with the approval of their Board of 
Directors, the broad Investment Policy and objectives to be achieved while undertaking investment 
transactions. 
The bank's investment policy is required to clearly  define the authority to put through deals, 
procedure to be followed for obtaining sanction of the appropriate authority, fixing various 
prudential exposure limits, and reporting system. A ll the transactions should be clearly recorded 
indicating full details. The top management should undertake a periodic review of investment 
transactions in a critical manner and put up large transactions to the Board, for information. 
The inter-bank Government securities transactions should be undertaken directly between banks 
and no bank should engage the services of any broke r in such transactions. Banks may, however, 
undertake Government securities transactions among themselves or with non-bank clients through 
members of the National Stock Exchange (NSE), the Stock Exchange, Mumbai (BSE)/OTC Exchange 
of India wherein the transactions are transparent. In case any transactions in Government securities are 
not undertaken on NSE, OTC Exchange of India or the  Stock Exchange, Mumbai (BSE), the same 
should be undertaken by the banks directly without the use of brokers. 
If a deal is put through with the help of a broker,  the role of the broker should be restricted to 
that of bringing the two parties to the deal togeth er. The brokers should not be involved in the 
settlement process at all, i.e., both the fund settlement and delivery of security s hould be done with 
the counterparty directly.

Bids for Natural Gas in Gujarat  
* 176. SHRI VIJAYKUMAR RUPANI: Will the Minister of  PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that Panna Mukta Tapti (PMT) JV partners invited the bids for sale of natural 
gas up to 4 Million Standard Cubic Metre per Day (MMSCMD) from 1st April, 2006 from various 
companies; 
 whether it is also a fact that Gujarat State Petrol eum Corporation Ltd., (GSPL) offered the 
highest price for gas amongst the bidders; 
 whether Government of Gujarat has made any representation to the Centre to follow the rules 
of tender and offer gas to GSPCL since their bid was the highest; and  
 what is the reaction of the Centre to the representation? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA): (a) to (d) Panna-
Mukta and Tapti (PMT) JV invited bids from the propospective buyers for sale of natural gas up to 4 
MMSCMD for a period of two years from 1.4.2006. 
In response to JV's bid GSPC, one of the bidders offered the highest price of US $ 4.75/ MMBTU 
for  4 MMSCMD gas. 
As per Production Sharing Contract (PSC) signed by the Government with PMT JV, the 
Government nominee for lifting of natural gas is GAIL. However, in view of lack of consensus on gas price 
between GAIL and PMT JV, the Government had allowed JV partners to market the gas directly initially 
for a period of one year with effect from 1.4.2005 and subsequently for another two years. However, to 
take care of the existing priority consumers in power and fertilizer sectors, GAIL continued to get major 
portion of the gas, while remaining gas was supplied in accordance with the bids received from the 
companies. 
The Government of Gujarat had represented to the Government of India. As per the PSC terms and 
provisions, Government nominee GAIL has the first right on natural gas produced from these PSCs. 
Accordingly, if GAIL is able to lift entire gas produced by PMT JV on terms, mutually agreeable to 
both the parties, GAIL may market the entire gas. The bids were invited from companies in 2006 in 
view of the lack of consensus on gas price between GAIL and PMT JV.

Linking of rivers  
t*179. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state:  
 whether Government has formulated any scheme to avoid drought and flood by linking 
various rivers of the country; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 the details of the rivers of Madhya Pradesh which are proposed to be linked; and 
 by when the work is likely to be started in regard? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ): (a) and (b) The Ministry of 
Water Resources (erstwhile Ministry of Irrigation) and Central Water Commission formulated a National 
Perspective Plan (NPP) for Water Resources Development in 1980. The NPP comprises of two 
components viz. (i) Peninsular Rivers Development a nd (ii) Himalayan Rivers Development and 
envisages construction of storages on various river systems along with interlinking canal systems to 
transfer water from water surplus areas to water deficit regions. National Water Development Agency 
(NWDA) was set up in 1982 to study the feasibility of Interbasin water transfer proposals and give a 
concrete shape to NPP. The Inter-linking proposals under NPP envisages additional benefits of 25 
million ha. of irrigation from surface waters, 10 million ha. by increased use of ground waters and 
generation of 34 Thousand MW of power apart from the incidental benefits of flood moderation, 
navigation, water supply, salinity & pollution control etc.  
Based on various studies conducted, NWDA has identified 30 links (16 in Peninsular Component 
and 14 in Himalayan Component) for preparation of Feasibility Reports (FRs). Out of these, FRs, of 14 
links under Peninsular Component and 2 links (Indian portion) under Himalayan Component have 
already been completed. NWDA has taken up the work of Preparation of Detailed Project Report 
(DPR) for one priority link viz. Ken-Betwa under Peninsular Component.

 The value of shares of listed companies is subject to the operational performance of the

not necessarily imply violation of the law but may be a reflection of several other factors, inspection 
under the provisions of Companies Act, 1956 in all such cases is not warranted. 
 The Securities Exchange Board of India (SEBI), has been set up under the Securities Exchange 
Board of India Act, 1992, as amended from time to time, to provide for the establishment of a Board 
to protect the interests of the investors in securi ties and to promote the development of, and to

carrying out market regulation in the interest of i nvestors and other stakeholders in accordance with 
the said Act by prescribing appropriate guidelines for observance by all participants in the capital 
market. 
In addition, the Companies Act, 1956 provides for a  legal framework for corporate governance 
that enables the shareholders of a company to parti cipate in decision making in a company in a 
democratic manner. The Companies Act, 1956 also provides a framework for prepration and disclosure 
of financial information of a company. 
To enable redressal of investors complaints a system for facilitating investors and depositors 
taelectronically lodge their complaints, with the G overnment has been put into place through the 
website of Ministry of Corporate Affairs(www.mca.gov.in ). The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has

Speculation on stock price  
1128. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 whether the stock holders such as Foreign Instituti onal Investors (FIIs) have a role in stock 
price overvaluation; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether it is a fact that above may cause more space for speculation; 
 if so, the details of appropriate cautionary stance taken to control the stock price speculation 
in the market; and 
 if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) The Stock Market is dynamic in nature and the market movement is influenced 
by demand and supply interplays as well as a host of other factors. 
The movement in stock market indices is a function of perception of the economy or a sector or 
of index stocks. It also depends on economic factor s, domestic and international events, market 
sentiments, level of floating stock available, corp orate performance and future economic growth. 
The stock market capitalizes and present and future  values of growth opportunities while 
evaluating the growth of all sectors in economy. 
The FIIs, cannot, therefore, be said to have a role in stock price overvaluation. 
(c) to (e) Speculative activities namely jobbing, d ay-trading and arbitragers are normal features 
of the Stock Market. By taking a position in the ma rket for the sake of profit the speculators bring 
to the market better information input and liquidity, thereby enabling the market to play an important 
economic function of price discovery and risk-management. It 

Written Answers to  [11 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions   77 
is manipulation, and not speculation, which is detr imental to the functioning of the market. The 
regulator, Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is concerned only with price manipulation. If 
any, SEBI keeps a constant vigil on the market, irrespective of the levels of the indices and has taken 
action wherever warranted.

Guidelines on One-Time Settlement Scheme for SME Accounts  
Please refer to Paragraph No. 8 of our circular RPCD.PLNFS.BC. No. 31/06.02.31/ 2005-06 
dated August 19,2005 and accordingly, a one-time settlement scheme for recovery of NPAs below Rs. 
10 crore is proposed hereunder which is required to be implemented by all public sector banks. These

2. The guidelines will not, however, cover cases of wilful default, fraud ano malfeasance, Banks 
shall identify cases of wilful default, fraud and m alfeasance and initiate prompt action. 
Accordingly, guidelines for one-time settlement of dues relating to NPAs of public sector bank in  
 sector are given below: 
(A) Guidelines for one-time settlement of chronic NPAs up to Rs. 10 crore  
[i] Coverage  
 The revised guidelines will cover all NPAs in SME sector which have become doubtful or loss as 
on March 31,2004 with outstanding balance of Rs. 10  crore and below on the date on which the 
account was classified as doubtful. 
 The guidelines will also cover NPAs classified as s ub-standard as on 31st March 2004, 
which have subsequently become doubtful or loss whe re the outstanding balance was Rs. 10 crore 
and below on the date on which the account was classified as doubtful. 
 These guidelines will cover cases on which the bank s have initiated action under the 
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 
and also cases pending before Courts/DRTs/BIFR, sub ject to consent decree being obtained from 
the Courts/DRTs/BIFR. 
 Cases of wilful default, fraud and malfeasance will not be covered. 
 The last date for receipt of applications from borr owers will be as at the close of business on 
March 31,2006. The processing under the revised guidelines shall be completed by June 30,2006. 
[ii] Settlement Formula — amount  
(a) NPAs classified as Doubtful or Loss as on March  31, 2004  
The minimum amount that shall be recovered under the revised guidelines in respect of one-time 
settlement of NPAs classified as doubtful or loss a s on March 31, 2004 will be 100% of the 
outstanding balance in the account as on the date on which the account was categorised as doubtful 
NPAs. 
(b) NPAs classified as sub-standard as on March 31, 2004 which became doubtful or loss 
subsequently  
The minimum amount that shall be recovered in respect of NPAs classified as substandard as on 
March 31,2004 which became doubtful or loss subsequ ently would be 100% of the outstanding 
balance in the account as on the date on which the account was categorised as doubtful NPAs, plus 
interest at existing Prime Lending Rate from April 1, 2004 till the date of final payment. 
 Payment  
The amount of settlement arrived at in both the above cases, shall preferably be paid in one lump 
sum. In cases where the borrowers are unable to pay  the entire amount in one lump sum, at least 
25% of the amount of settlement shall be paid upfro nt and the balance amount of 75% should be 
recovered in instalments within a period of one year together with interest at the existing Prime Lending 
Rate from the date of settlement up to the date of final payment.

Debt restructuring mechanism for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs)-
Announcement made by Union Finance Minister  
As part of announcement made by the Hon'ble Finance Minister for improving flow of 

Written Answers to  [11 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions   87 
credit to small and medium enterprises, a debt rest ructuring mechanism for units in SME sector is 
required to be implemented by all banks. These deta iled guidelines are being issued to ensure 
restructuring of debt of all eligible small and med ium enterprises at terms which are, at least, as 
favourable as the Corporate Debt Restructuring mechanism in the banking sector. 
2. Definition of SMEs  
SMEs will be as defined in RPCD Circular No. RPCD. PLFNS. BC. 31/06.02.31/2005-06 dated 
August 19,2005, which is reproduced below: 
"At present, a small scale industrial unit is an un dertaking in which investment in plant and 
machinery, does not exceed Rs. 1 crore, except in r espect of certain specified items under 
hosiery, hand tools, drugs and pharmaceuticals, sta tionery items and sports goods, where 
this investment limit has been enhanced to Rs. 5 cr ore. A comprehensive legislation which 
would enable the paradigm shift from small scale in dustry to small and medium enterprises is 
under consideration of Parliament. Pending enactment of the above legislation, current SSI/tiny 
industries definition may continue Units with investment in plant and machinery in excess of 
SSI limit and up to Rs 10 crore may be treated as medium Enterprises (ME)." 
3. Eligibility criteria  
(i) These guidelines would be applicable to the following entities, which are viable or potentially 
viable: 
a. All non-corporate SMEs irrespective of the level  of dues to banks. 
b. All corporate SMEs, which are enjoying banking f acilities from a single bank, 
irrespective of the level of dues to the bank. 
c. All corporate SMEs, which have funded and non-fu nded outstanding up to 
Rs. 10 crore under multiple/consortium banking arra ngement (for outstanding of 
Rs. 10 crore and above, guidelines are being issued separately). 
(ii) Accounts involving wilful default, fraud and malfeasance will not be eligible for restructuring 
under these guidelines. 
(iii) Accounts classified by banks as "Loss Assets" will not be eligible for restructuring. 
(iv) In respect of BIFR cases banks should ensure completion of all formalities in seeking approval 
from BIFR before implementing the package. 
4. Viability criteria  
Banks may decide on the acceptable viability benchm ark, consistent with the unit becoming 
viable in 7 years and the repayment period for restructured debt not exceeding 10 years. 
5. Prudential Norms for restructured accounts  
(i) Treatment of 'standard' accounts subjected to restructuring  
(a) A rescheduling of the instalments of principal alone, would not cause a standard asset to be 
classified in the sub-standard category, provided the borrower's outstanding is 
 

88   Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
fully covered by tangible security. However, the condition of tangible security may not be made 
applicable in cases where the outstanding is up to Rs. 5 lakh, since the collateral requirement 
for loans up to Rs. 5 lakh has been dispensed with for SSI/tiny sector.  
 A rescheduling of interest element would not cause an asset to be downgraded to 
substandard category subject to the condition that the amount of sacrifice, if any, in the element of 
interest, measured in present value terms, is eithe r written off or provision is made to the extent of  
the sacrifice involved. 
 In case there is a sacrifice involved in the amount  of interest in present value terms, as at (b) 
above, the amount of sacrifice should either be wri tten off or provision made to the extent of the 
sacrifice involved. 
(ii) Treatment of 'sub-standard'/'doubtful' accounts subject to restructuring  
(a) A rescheduling of the instalments of principal alone, would render a 'sub-standard,/ 'doubtful' 
asset eligible to continue in the 'sub-standard'/'doubtful' category for the specified period (as defined 
in paragraph 7 below), provided the borrower's outs tanding, is fully covered by tangible security, 
However, the condition of tangible security may not  be made applicable in cases where the 
outstanding is up to Rs. 5 lakh, since the collater al requirement for loans up to Rs. 5 lakh has 
been dispensed with for SSI/tiny sector.  
 A rescheduling of interest element would render a s ub-standard/'doubtful' asset eligible to be 
continued to be classified in sub-standard/'doubtfu l' category for the specified period subject to the 
condition that the amount of sacrifice, if any, in the element of interest, measured in present value terms, 
is either written off or provision is made to the extent of the sacrifice involved. 
 Even in cases where the sacrifice is by way of writ e off of the past interest dues, the asset 
should continue to be treated as sub-standard/'doubtful'. 
(iii) Treatment of Provision  
 Provision made towards interest sacrifice should be created by debit to Profit & Loss account 
and held in a distinct account. For this purpose, t he future interest due as per current BPLR in 
respect of an account should be discounted to the p resent value at a rate appropriate to the risk 
category of the borrower (i.e., current PLR + the a ppropriate term premium and credit risk premium 
for the borrower-category) and compared with the present value of the dues expected to be received 
under the restructuring package, discounted on the same basis. 
 Sacrifice may be re-computed on each balance sheet date till satisfactory completion of all 
repayment obligations and full repayment of the out standing in the account, so as to capture the 
changes in the fair value on account of changes in BPLR, term premium and the credit category of the 
borrower Consequently, banks may provide for the shortfall in provision of reverse the amount of excess 
provision held in the distinct account. 
 The amount of provision made for NPA, may be revers ed when the account is re-classifed as 
a 'standard asset'. 
6. Additional finance  
Additional finance, if any, may be treated as 'standard asset' in all accounts, viz., standard, 

Written Answers to  [11 MARCH, 2008]  Unstarred Questions   89 
sub-standard, and doubtful accounts, up to a period of one year after the date when first payment of 
interest or of principal, whichever is earlier, fal ls due under the approved restructuring package. If  
the restructured asset does not qualify for upgrada tion at the end of the above period additional 
finance shall be placed in the same asset classification category as the restructured debt. 
7. Upgradation of restructured accounts  
The sub-standard/doubtful accounts at para 5 (ii) ( a) & (b) above, which have been subjected to 
restructuring, whether in respect of principal instalment of interest, by whatever modality, would be 
eligible to be upgraded to the standard category af ter the specified period, i.e. a period of one year 
after the date when first payment of interest or of  principal, whichever is earlier, falls due under the 
rescheduled terms, subject to satisfactory performance during the period. 
8. Asset classification status  
During the specified one-year period, the asset cla ssification status of rescheduled accounts will 
not deteriorate if satisfactory performance of the account is demonstrated during the period. In case, 
however, the satisfactory performance during the on e year period is not evidenced the asset 
classification of the restructured account would be  governed as per the applicable prudential norms 
with reference to the pre-restructuring payment sch edule. The asset classification would be bank-
specific based on record of recovery of each bank, as per the existing prudential norms applicable 
to banks. 
9. Repeated restructuring  
The special dispensation for asset classification a s available in terms of paragraphs 5,6 and 7 
above, shall be available only when the account is restructured for the first time. 
10. Procedure  
(i) Based on these guidelines, banks may formulate, with the approval of their Board of Directors, 
a debt restructuring scheme or SMEs. While framing the scheme, banks may ensure that the 
scheme is simple to comprehend and will, at the min imum, include parameters indicated in 
these guidelines. 
(ii) The restructuring would follow a receipt of a request to that effect from the borrowing units. 
(iii) In case of eligible SMEs which are under consortium/multiple banking arrangements, the bank 
with the maximum outstanding may work out the restructuring package, along with the bank 
having the second largest share. 
//. Timeframe  
Banks should work out the restructuring package and  implement the same within a maximum 
period of 60 days from date of receipt of requests. 
12. Review  
Banks may review the progress in rehabilitation and  restructuring of SM accounts on quarterly 
basis and keep the Board informed. '

t 1144. SHRI AJAY SINGH CHAUTALA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:

method of recovery? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that incidents of alleged use of 
coercive methods by some banks for recovery of loans in case of default has come to their notice. 
However, details in this regard are not collated by RBI.  
(c) The complaints have been taken up by RBI with the concerned banks for appropriate action. In 
case of any violation of extant guidelines by a bank, appropriate regulatory action is taken by RBI.  
Guidelines have already been formulated by RBI on Fair Practice Code for Lenders in May, 2003, 
which inter-alia, stipulate that in the matter of recovery of loans, the lender should not resort to 
undue harassment viz. persistently bothering the borrowers at odd hours, use of muscle power for 
recovery of loans etc.  
RBI has also issued instructions to all commercial banks/NBFCs (excluding Regional Rural 
Banks) in November, 2005 regarding Credit Card Operations, which clearly stipulate that their agents 
should not resort to intimidation or harassment of any kind, either verbal or physical, against any 
person in their debt collection efforts. This includes acts intending to humiliate publicly or intrude 
upon privacy of the debtors, their family members, referees and friends, making threatening and 
anonymous calls or making false and misleading representations.  
The Code of Banks' Commitments to Customers formulated by Banking Codes and Standard 
Boards of India (BCSBI) provides, inter-alia, that the collection policy of the bank be built on 
courtesy, fair treatment and persuasion and the bank follows a security repossession policy in 
consonance with the law.  
The IBA has also formulated a "Model Code for collection of dues and repossession of Security" 
which has been recommended to banks for adoption and implementation. The Model Code, inter-alia, 
provides that banks commit to maintaining the dignity and respect of customers in their Debt 
Collection Policy and not follow policies that are unduly coercive in collection of dues.  
Further, in Mid-Term Review of Annual Policy Statement (dated October 30,2007), RBI has 
observed that in view of the rise in the number of litigations against banks for engaging recovery agents 
in the recent past, it is felt that the adverse publicity could result in serious reputational risk for the 
banking sector as a whole. RBI has urged banks to follow prescribed specific considerations while 
engaging recovery agents. RBI has stated that complaints received regarding abusive practices 
followed by a bank's recovery agent would invite se rious supervisory disapproval. RBI would 
consider imposing a temporary ban (or even a

Loans to IIFCL from forex reserve 
1159. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 whether it has been decided to disburse a loan of USD Five billion to India Infrastructure Finance 
Co. Ltd. (IIFCL) by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) out of the forex reserve; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 the magnitude of tangible benefit estimated, if any, to be accruing to the forex reserve by the 
proposed lending of IIFCL; 
 the nature and dimension of risks which the loan would be exposed; and 
 the details of the precaution envisaged, if any, to cover such risks adequately? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): 
(a) and (b) As per information received from RBI, a decision has been taken to invest up to USD 5 
billion in US dollar denominated bonds issued by th e Wholly Owned Overseas Subsidiary/Special 
Purpose Vehicle (SPV) of the India Infrastructure F inance Company Limited (IIFCL) using a part 
of the foreign exchange reserves. The overseas subsidiary/SPV of IIFCL will issue 10-year maturity 
US dollar denominated bonds with a face value of US D one million with the maximum aggregate 
issuance of USD 5 billion. These bonds will be fully guaranteed by the Government of India for both 
principal and interest. The bonds will carry a floating rate of interest equivalent to the USD six month 
LIBOR and will be reset every six months. 
The SPV will lend in foreign currency to Indian companies implementing infrastructure projects in 
India for import of capital goods solely for capital expenditure outside India. 
(c) to (e) Since the bonds are guaranteed by Government of India for payment of both principal 
and interest no risk to RBI is envisaged.

Fake companies operating in stock markets 
1163. SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware that a large number  of fake companies had entered into 
the share market and engaging in wrong dealing; 
 if so, whether Government has taken any steps to prevent entry of such fake companies; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): 
(a) As and when any such instance is noticed, Ministry of Corporate Affairs and SEBI take appropriate 
action under the Companies Act and the securities laws. However, the question presumably refers to 
the companies which raised funds from public throug h IPOs and subsequently failed, inter-alia, to 
comply with the listing/filing requirements of Registrar of Companies and the Stock Exchanges for 
a period of two years and were not found at their r egistered office address at the time of inspection 
done by Stock Exchange. These companies are known a s "vanishing companies" as per the 
categorization adopted by Coordination and Monitori ng Committee (CMC), a joint mechanism 
between the SEBI and the Ministry of Corporate Affa irs (MCA). These companies are being 
identified in phases. So far such companies who made IPOs during 1992—2001 have been identified. 
As on date, there are 122 companies identified as "vanishing companies." 
(b) and (c) In addition to actions taken by MCA, SE BI has issued orders against 102 vanishing 
companies and 391 directors/promoters prohibiting them from associating in any way with the capital 
market activities and accessing the capital market for a period of five years. Merchant banker 
managing the issue is required to check the anteced ents of the promoters/directors of the company 
and have to confirm that none of them has been debarred by SEBI. Besides, SEBI has strengthened the 
eligibility requirements for accessing capital market.

Funding of MFIs  
1164. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 how many private banks are funding Micro Finance In stitutions (MFIs) in Uttar Pradesh 
(UP) and whether their interest rates are very high and how many MFIs are there in UP; 
 whether Government would establish a non-profit micro credit institution for women in North 
India particularly in rural sector; 
 how many women self help groups linked to micro fin ance are there in Uttar Pradesh and 
Chhattisgarh; 
(d) what Government is doing to boost micro finance  movement in these States, 
particularly amongst women; and 
(e) how many families of these States have been linked to micro finance credit? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) Many Private/Foreign Banks like ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, ING Vysya Bank, ABN 
AMRO, Citi Bank, Axis Bank etc. are financing Micro Finance Institutions (MFIs) in UP. The rate of 
interest charged by banks including Private Banks for all purposes including Micro credit has been 
deregulated by Reserve Bank of India. As per provis ional data available, 12 MFIs are functioning 
in UP. 
 The Government has introduced a bill in Lok Sabha o n 20.03.2007 called "The Micro 
Financial Sector (Development and Regulation) Bill,  2007" to create environment friendly policy 
for micro-finance services in the country. The bill  is intended to provide a formal statutory 
framework for the promotion, development and regula tion of the micro finance sector. As of now 
there is no plan of the Government to establish any micro finance institution. 
 The number of Self Help Groups (SHGs) credit linked  to banks (as on 31.03.2007) in Uttar 
Pradesh and Chhattisgarh is 1,98,587 and 41,703 res pectively. Of this around 90% of SHGs are 
women groups. 
 The Self Help Group (SHG) Bank Linkage Programme, facilitated by NABARD since 1992, 
is the flagship micro finance programme in the coun try. Both the States i.e. UP and Chhattisgarh 
have been identified among the priority states by N ABARD for promotion and linkage of the 
SHGs. Special attention is being provided for capac ity building of various stakeholders of the 
programme and for roping in new partners and suppor ting existing partners for promotion and 
linkage of SHGs by way of grant assistance in these States. 
 The estimated number of families credit linked to banks (as on 31.03.2007) under SHG bank 
linkage programme in Uttar Pradesh and Chhattisgarh is 27.8 lakh and 5.83 lakh respectively.

1165. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
 what is the total level of inflation during the current financial year; 
 what are the major factors which are responsible for high rate of inflation; 
 what steps are being taken to control the inflationary trend in the country; and 
 what are the main impacts of the inflation of the common man? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) The cumulative inflation in terms of WPI (since 1 st week of April, 2007 to 
February 23, 2008) was 4.33 per cent during the cur rent financial year 2007-08, which is lower 
than 5.98 per cent as on 24 February, 2007 in the last financial year 2006-07. 
(c) and (d) Containment of inflation remains high o n the agenda of the Government. Anti-
inflationary policies of the government include str ict fiscal discipline, rationalization of duties of  
essential items, effective supply-demand management of essential commodities through liberal tariff 
and trade policies, and strengthening the public di stribution system. The Monetary policy of Reserve 
Bank of India, while being conductive to economic g rowth, has attempted to contain inflationary 
expectations arising out of uncertainties in domestic and international environment.

Asset Reconstruction Companies  
1176. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRA SEKHAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that the default retail debts amounting to hundreds of crores have been 
transferred by private/Government Banks to Asset Reconstruction Companies; 
 what is the actual total amount of retail assets go ne bad transferred to Asset 
Reconstruction Companies; 
 who is responsible for overseeing Asset Reconstruction Companies and how do they recover 
these bad loans; 
 whether it is also a fact that these Asset Reconstruction Companies are in turn often selling 
these bad debts at huge discount; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): 
(a) and (b) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that till December 31,2007 default retail debts 
amounting to Rs. 36,235.56 Crore (Book value) have been transferred by the private/Government 
Banks/Financial Institutions (FIs) to six Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) registered with 
RBI, at an acquisition price of Rs. 9,159.73 Crore. 
(c) RBI is responsible for overseeing the operations of ARCs. These companies are granted the 
Certificate of Registration by RBI under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and 
Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act, 2002).  
RBI has prescribed detailed guidelines on sale of financial assets by banks/FIs to Securitisation 
Company (SC)/Reconstruction Company (RC) vide Circular dated April 23, 2003. These guidelines 
prescribed the following:  

122 Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
The SARFAESI Act, 2002 allows acquisition of financial assets by SC/RC from any bank/ FI on such 
terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between them. This provides for sale of the financial 
assets on 'without recourse' basis, i.e. with the entire credit risk associated with the financial assets being 
transferred to SC/RC, as well as on 'with recourse' basis, i.e., subject to unrealized part of the asset 
reverting to the seller bank/FI. They are, however,  directed to ensure that the effect of the sale of 
the financial assets should be such that the asset is taken off their books. After the sale there should not 
be any known liability devolving on the banks/FIs. 
Banks/FIs, which propose to sell to SC/RC their fin ancial assets should ensure that the sale is 
conducted in a prudent manner in accordance with a policy approved by their Board. The Board shall 
lay down policies and gidelines covering, inter alia, financial assets to be sold, norms and procedure 
for sale of such financial assets, valuation proced ure to be followed and delegation of powers of 
various functionaries. 
Each bank/FI will make its own assessment of the va lue offered by the SC/RC for the financial 
asset and decide whether to accept or reject the of fer. Under no circumstances can a transfer to the 
SC/RC be made at a contingent price whereby in the event of shortfall in the realization by the SC/RC, 
the banks/FIs would have to bear a part of the shortfall. 
(d) and (e) Since ARCs operate on commercial lines it is unlikely that assets at huge discounts 
to purchase value are sold.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS 
(SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. Conseq uent to the Supreme Court order dated 
22.11.2001 in Writ Petition 13029/85, the Environme ntal Pollution (Prevention and Control) 
Authority for the National Capital Region has directed Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) 
to carry out an investigation on fuel adulteration.  The details of the recommendations made by 
CSE in section 9 of the Report is given in the Statement. (See below) 
(c) and (d) Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) undertake regular and surprise inspections of Retail 
Outlets and also take action under Marketing Discip line Guidelines (MDG) and Dealership 
Agreements against those indulging in adulteration and malpractices. MDG provide for termination 
of dealership in the first instance itself for serious malpractices like adulteration, tampering of seals, 
and unauthorized fittings/gears in dispensing units. 
In spite of above, the possibility of adulteration of petrol/diesel by some unscrupulous elements 
cannot be ruled out due to huge price difference between petrol/diesel and various adulterants available 
in the market and the easy miscibility of these products with petrol/ diesel. 
In order to check adulteration, the Government has taken a number of additional initiatives viz., 
Automation of Retail Outlets, Third party certification of Retail Outlets, Monitoring of movement of 
tank trucks through Global Positioning System (GPS), Jan Kerosene Pariyojna (JKP), Use of Marker in 
Kerosene, Revision of MDG etc. 
Statement  
Details of the recommendations made by CSE  
"Recommendations  
Our investigation shows that the current product quality monitoring system is extremely weak and 
stems largely from weak regulations and enforcement , skewed market prices of the petroleum 
products and lack of accountability in the petroleum sector. Unless this is corrected the root cause of 
the problem cannot be eliminated. Immediate direction is needed in the operational, technical and 
economic areas. While there is a unanimous agreement that skewed prices are responsible for 
adulteration, so far no solutions have been possible for political reasons. This study clearly shows that 
unless we take serious steps to improve the system to prevent and check adulteration, we will not even 
begin to touch the profitable business of adulteration. The current system is compromised from testing 
methods that are not adequate to detect adulteration to penalty syst ems designed to let the 
manufacturers go scot-free. It is possible to create a library of  different refinery samples of 
automotive fuels and possible adulterants. With the help of the standard library chromatogram it will be 
much easier to detect fuel adulteration. 
Make oil companies accountable for the quality of fuel at the retail end  
Any extent of vigilance and surveillance will be meaningless unless strict liability is imposed on 
the oil companies to take full responsibility for the quality of fuels they sell at their retail outlets. As 
of now the responsibility and penalty are all fragmented along with supply chain. Though retailers 
and the transporters are penalized by the oil companies if malpractices occur, the oil companies are 
not held accountable. To put it simply consumers 

136 Written Answers to  [R A J Y A  SA B HA ]  Unstarred Questions  
cannot sue the oil companies for adulterated fuels. Unless this is done checks and balance in the system will not 
work effectively to prevent malpractices at any level. The best way that consumer pressure can be intensified on 
the oil companies is to develop a system of public rating of the retail outlets by the name of the oil companies on a 
monthly basis based on an independent inspection, testing and audit of the outlet. 
In a competitive market there are multiple oil companies rivaling for market share. This will become more 
severe with decontrol of the petroleum sector soon. In such a situation protection of brand name would be most 
critical for the oil companies to guard their market share. Therefore, quality based public rating of the retail outlets 
by the name of companies would work best in disciplining the supply chain and preventing the widespread 
malady. 
Improve testing procedures and tighten fuel quality standards  
Immediate attention should be paid to tightening the fuel quality standards and regulating some key parameters 
that are not done today like aromatics, olefins in petrol, and PAH in diesel. Even the broad range that is allowed 
under the current specifications should be adequately tightened. Tighter the net easier it is to catch dubious 
samples. 
« 
Develop alternative testing procedures for more accurate detection  
F6r more accurate detection alternative testing methods and protocols should be adopted straight away and 
applied for surveillance."
